stimulus.source_note: Original secondary passage written for this question, summarizing Barron's Premium 2027 Chapter 3, Topic 1.5 and Topic 1.6; Princeton Review Chapter 6.
stimulus.text: In Spain's American colonies, Spaniards were always greatly outnumbered by Native peoples, and Spanish men greatly outnumbered Spanish women. In these circumstances, intermarriage was common. The children of Spanish men and Indigenous women were called mestizos, and they made up four to five percent of the population. The children of Spanish men and African women were called mulattos. Over time, mixing produced a large population of people of mixed ancestry.

stem: Over time, intermarriage produced a large population of mestizos and mulattos. What did this growth change in Spanish America?

options.text: It created new social categories that had not existed before.

options.misconception: Mixing produced the categories of the casta system; it did not end ranking by ancestry.
options.text: It ended the system that ranked people by ancestry.

options.misconception: Spaniards stayed a tiny minority, one or two percent, even as mixed populations grew.
options.text: It made Spaniards the majority of the colonial population.

options.misconception: Mixing continued and the categories kept multiplying; it never stopped.
options.text: It stopped all further mixing between peoples.

instruction: Answer from the stimulus and stem only. Pick one option. Do not open the question file.
